title: Faith with little ones, ages 3 to 6
subtitle: Eight sessions for parents of children from three to six: what a small child can take in, Bible stories at bedtime, first prayers, songs, wonder, grace when they do wrong, church with wiggles, and where God is.
intro: This track is for anyone raising children from about three to six: a mother or a father, a single parent, a grandparent raising grandchildren, an adoptive or foster parent, or a parent whose husband or wife doesn't share the faith. It sits in Faith at Home beside Start at the table tonight and For parents: leading faith at home, and it gets down to the height of a child who still needs help with buttons.

There are eight sessions of about ten minutes. Each gives you a short teaching, one page on this site to open, one question for you, one thing to try with your child that week, and a verse to keep. Nothing here is a test of your parenting. Little children forget, wriggle, and ask for the same story six nights running, and all of that counts.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a group of parents of small children through Faith with little ones, ages 3 to 6, or two parents taking it together. The group is for mothers, fathers, grandparents, adoptive and foster parents, and anyone else raising a child under seven, whether they grew up in church or never saw faith at home at all. A leader doesn't need tidy children or a quiet house. A leader needs to be honest about their own tired evenings and gentle with everyone else's.

Each person reads the session and opens its page before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It talks over what happened at home that week, the good bedtimes and the ones that dissolved, using the group guide for each session, gathered below in order.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten parents is a good size. Meet for about an hour, once a week or once a fortnight, for eight meetings, and finish when you promised, because small children wake early and babysitters go home. Make room for single parents, for parents whose spouse doesn't share their faith, and for grandparents raising grandchildren. None of them should feel like the exception in the room.

sections.title: The room
body: A living room or kitchen table works well, and childcare in another room helps parents listen. If small children have to be present, let that be fine; a group for parents of little ones will be interrupted. Say at the first meeting that no one's family is on trial, that anyone may pass on any question, that what is said stays in the room unless someone is in danger, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About an hour, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Ten minutes: how last week's one thing to try went at home, including the nights it fell apart.
Five minutes: one person reads the session's verse aloud.
Twenty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order, with room for what parents bring.
Ten minutes: the prayer prompt, praying for children by name. Nobody has to pray aloud.
Name the next session and its one thing to try, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Parents of small children ask practical questions that turn out to be deep ones: whether to make a child pray, what to say when a pet dies, whether a three-year-old can believe, when a child is ready for the Lord's Supper or for baptism. Don't hand out formulas. Say what Christians share, that God welcomes children and that faith is his gift, and say honestly where faithful churches differ.

On the baptism of infants, the age of communion and methods of discipline, faithful parents hold different views. The track takes no side on these, and the group shouldn't either. Send each family to their own pastor and their own church's practice.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: A group of parents of young children will meet real weight: exhaustion that has gone on for years, a child with a disability or an illness, a marriage under strain, a miscarriage or the loss of a child, a parent raising children alone after a death or a divorce. When that comes into the room, stop and listen. Don't explain it and don't hurry back to the session. Ask whether the group should go on or pause, and speak with the person afterwards.

If anyone says that a child is being harmed, or that they or a child are not safe at home, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. A child who may be in danger is a matter for the police and child protection services, not only for the group.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point a parent to Find Help when what they carry has grown too heavy: anger at home that someone cannot control, harm done to a child, a marriage where someone is afraid, exhaustion or sadness that has taken their sleep and will not lift, or a parent who no longer wants to go on. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor.

sessions.title: What a small child can take in
teaching: A three-year-old won't follow an argument, but faith doesn't have to wait until they can. Small children learn through story, song, repetition and touch, through what happens again and again in the arms of people they trust. They can learn that God made them, that he loves them, and that he is near, long before they can explain any of it. The family catechism begins with a question a child of three can answer, and the short answer it teaches is four words long. The faith of the whole church stands behind those four words.

So aim low and often: a few sentences, a picture, a song, a short prayer, and the same again tomorrow. Jesus didn't wait for children to understand before he welcomed them. “And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them” (Mark 10:16). His disciples thought the children were in the way, and he thought they belonged right there. A small child takes in a great deal of a parent's faith simply by being held and blessed by someone who believes it.

open.label: Parenting Young Children
open.why: What Scripture says about the early years: not a delay before the real parenting begins, but the slow shaping of a small soul in ordinary moments.

also.label: Question 1: Who made you?
also.why: The first question of the family catechism, with a short answer a three-year-old can learn by heart and a verse to go with it.

also.label: Made on Purpose
also.why: A family devotion on Psalm 139 for the youngest at the table: God made you on purpose, and he likes what he made.

sessions.question: What does your child already know about God, from what they have seen and heard in your home?
sessions.do: Each day this week, ask your child who made them, and teach them the catechism's short answer. Then at bedtime put a hand on their head and bless them in one sentence.

verse.text: And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them.

group.open: What is your earliest memory of hearing about God, and who was it from?
discuss: Why do you think the disciples saw the children as being in the way?
What can a three-year-old take in about God that adults sometimes forget?
Which parts of a small child's day already repeat, and how could faith ride along with them?
group.pray: Pray for each small child in the group's homes by name, and give thanks that Jesus welcomes children long before they understand anything.

sessions.title: Bible stories at bedtime
teaching: Children are made for stories, and the Bible is mostly story. The how-to this session opens says to start where the story is strongest, read short and often, and stop while attention is still alive. Five verses every day forms a child more than three chapters once a month. A good illustrated story Bible is a fine way in for the very young, as long as it stays close to the text and doesn't flatten every story into a lesson about being good.

The best story Bibles read Scripture the way Jesus read it. On the road to Emmaus, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself” (Luke 24:27). Noah, Abraham, Joseph and David aren't a row of heroes to copy. Each is part of one story that is going somewhere, to the rescue God works through his Son. After the story, ask what happened, let your child tell it back, and point once to Jesus. One sentence is enough.

open.label: How to Read the Bible With Young Children
open.why: How to start with story, read short and often, ask rather than lecture, and avoid raising a child on a Bible where nothing is at stake.

also.label: The Bible's story: Christ
also.why: For you: the part of the Bible's one story that every other part leads to, to read before you tell any of it at bedtime.

also.label: The One Who Comes Looking
also.why: A devotion on Jesus the good shepherd, a picture a small child can hold: someone who leads them and comes looking when they wander.

sessions.question: Which Bible story did you love as a child, or would have loved, and where does it point to Jesus?
sessions.do: Choose a bedtime this week. Read one short Bible story aloud, ask your child what happened, let them tell it back to you, and say one sentence about how the story points to Jesus.

verse.text: And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself.

group.open: What stories were read to you at bedtime when you were small?
discuss: What is lost when every Bible story is turned into a lesson about being good?
How would you tell the story of Noah or David so that it points to Jesus without forcing it?
What gets in the way of a few minutes of reading at bedtime in your home?
group.pray: Pray for the bedtimes in each home this week, that tired parents would find a few minutes to read and that children would hear of Jesus.

sessions.title: Praying with a three-year-old
teaching: A three-year-old's prayer is short, and it is still prayer. Small children learn to pray mostly by hearing the people they live with pray, and the end of the day is when they finally stop moving. The how-to this session opens gives a pattern that lasts for years: thank God for one good thing from the day, say sorry for one thing, ask for help with one thing tomorrow, and then bless the child. Keep it the same most nights, because the repetition is the teaching.

With the very young, let them repeat a short line after you, then let them try their own. Thanks for the dog is a real prayer. Pray plainly, the way you'd talk to someone who loves you, and don't perform. When the dark brings worries, hand them to God together. A psalm long prayed at the close of the day puts it in one line: “I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8). A child who hears that every night is learning who stays awake while they sleep.

open.label: How to Pray With Your Kids at Bedtime
open.why: A simple pattern for bedtime prayer that a child can keep for years: one thanks, one sorry, one request for tomorrow, and a blessing.

also.label: Pray Psalm 4 slowly
also.why: An evening psalm to pray slowly on your own, before you pray its last verse over a child who is falling asleep.

also.label: Question 53: What is prayer?
also.why: The catechism's short answer for a child, that prayer is talking with God, who loves to hear us, with a verse beside it.

sessions.question: What would you most like your child to know about God when they lie awake in the dark?
sessions.do: For five nights, pray with your child at bedtime using the pattern: one thanks, one sorry, one thing to ask help with tomorrow. Then put a hand on their head and bless them.

verse.text: I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.

group.open: Did anyone pray with you at bedtime as a child, and what do you remember of it?
discuss: Why does a pattern repeated every night teach a small child so much?
What does a child learn from hearing a parent say sorry to God?
How could a parent who feels awkward praying aloud begin anyway?
group.pray: Pray for the nights in each home, for children who don't like the dark, and for parents who feel too tired to pray at all.

sessions.title: Singing and memorizing
teaching: Small children learn by heart without trying. They pick up the words of an advertisement after hearing it twice and sing the same song all afternoon. That gift is worth spending on something that will last. God's people have always sung their faith, from the psalms of Israel to the hymns of the early church, and for most of the church's history believers learned their faith by heart long before many of them could read. Paul puts teaching and singing in one breath, “as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God” (Colossians 3:16).

Choose one short verse and one song and repeat them for a month. Sing in the car and at bath time. Say the verse at breakfast, leave off the last word, and let your child fill it in. The memory tool this session opens brings a verse back after one, three, seven, fourteen and thirty days, because that's how memory holds. Use it to learn the verse yourself first, so that it's on your lips when your child needs it. Words learned at four can still be there at forty.

open.label: Memorize Scripture
open.why: A tool that brings a verse back after one, three, seven, fourteen and thirty days, so you know it well enough to teach it.

also.label: The family catechism
also.why: Short answers for children, with a way to practise saying them aloud one question at a time, good for learning by heart together.

also.label: How to Memorize Scripture
also.why: For the parent: why memorizing Scripture is worth the effort, and plain ways to keep a verse once you have learned it.

sessions.question: What song or verse do you still know by heart from childhood, and how did it get there?
sessions.do: Choose one short verse to learn with your child this month. Say it at breakfast each day, leaving off the last word for them to finish, and sing one song about God together in the car.

verse.text: Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God.

group.open: What song from your childhood can you still sing all the way through?
discuss: Why do you think God's people have always sung their faith rather than only saying it?
Which short verse would you most want your child to carry into adult life?
How can learning by heart stay a joy for a small child rather than a chore?
group.pray: Give thanks for the songs and verses that were handed to you, and pray that the words your children learn now would stay with them for life.

sessions.title: God made everything
teaching: Small children are natural noticers. They stop for a beetle, ask why the moon follows the car, and want to know where rain comes from. Wonder is one of the first ways a child meets God, and a parent doesn't need to manufacture it. The parent's part is to slow down enough to notice what the child has noticed, and to give it a name. The psalmist did exactly that: “How many are Your works, O LORD! In wisdom You have made them all; the earth is full of Your creatures” (Psalm 104:24).

The devotion this session opens starts at the beginning: the world was spoken into being by a God who meant to make it and called it good. Read Genesis 1 in pieces, one day at a time, and go outside afterwards to look for what God made on that day. Every person was made in his image too, which is why the child who stops for a beetle can also learn to stop for the child standing alone at the edge of the playground. Wonder at the world and care for people grow from the same root.

open.label: God Called It Good
open.why: A family devotion on Genesis 1, with a passage to read aloud, questions for the youngest, and something to do together.

also.label: Psalm 104, passage by passage
also.why: A whole psalm of wonder at what God made, from the sea creatures to the bread on the table, with plain-words notes.

also.label: Creation
also.why: For the parent who wants more: what the whole Bible teaches about creation, traced through Scripture in the Study Bible.

sessions.question: When did your child last stop to wonder at something, and what did you do?
sessions.do: Take a slow walk with your child this week and let them set the pace. When they stop to look at something, look too, and tell them that God made it and called it good.

verse.text: How many are Your works, O LORD! In wisdom You have made them all; the earth is full of Your creatures.

group.open: What in creation still makes you stop and stare?
discuss: Why might a hurried parent miss the very moments when a child is ready to wonder?
How does knowing God made everything shape the way a child treats animals, the world and other people?
What would a slower week look like in your home?
group.pray: Give thanks for the things your children noticed this week, and pray for parents to slow down enough to wonder with them.

sessions.title: When they do wrong
teaching: Every small child does wrong, often loudly and in public. They grab, hit, fib about the biscuit and refuse to share. A parent's correction matters, and so does what the child learns about God through it. The family catechism gives a small child something to say: what should we do when we sin? We tell God we are sorry, and he forgives us because of Jesus. The aim of correction isn't a child who hides wrongdoing to stay out of trouble. It's a child who learns that a wrong can be named, forgiven and put right.

So correct calmly, clearly and briefly, and then close it. Say what was wrong, give a fitting consequence, help them say sorry and make it right, then hug them and let it be finished, with no grudge carried to supper. Jesus told of a son who wasted everything and a father who ran to meet him (Luke 15:20). A child corrected by a parent who restores them quickly learns both halves of that story. Christian parents differ on methods, but no child should be afraid of a parent's anger. And when you get it wrong, say sorry to your child.

open.label: Question 59: What should we do when we sin?
open.why: A short answer a small child can learn and say after doing wrong: we tell God we are sorry, and he forgives us because of Jesus.

also.label: The Father Who Runs
also.why: A devotion on the father in Jesus' story who runs to meet his son, for reading together at the end of a hard day.

also.label: Parenting Struggles
also.why: What Scripture says to a parent worn down by the daily battles of raising children, gathered in one place.

sessions.question: After your child does wrong, what do they usually learn about you, and what would you want them to learn about God?
sessions.do: Next time your child does wrong, correct them calmly, help them say sorry and put it right, then hug them and say plainly that it's finished. If you owe them an apology, give it.

verse.text: As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him.

care: If anger has become something you cannot control, or if anger at home has made anyone afraid, that is more than a verse can fix. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: How were you corrected as a small child, and what did it teach you?
discuss: What is the difference between a child who is sorry and a child who is only afraid of trouble?
Why does closing a correction quickly matter so much to a small child?
What might your child learn from hearing you apologize to them?
group.pray: Pray for patience in each home, for parents who lose their temper, and for children to know they are loved after they do wrong.

sessions.title: Church with wiggly children
teaching: Taking a small child to church can feel like an hour of shushing, and some families stop going for a season because it's simply too hard. But children belong in the church. When the disciples tried to keep children away, Jesus was indignant and said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these” (Mark 10:14). A wriggling four-year-old in a pew isn't an interruption of the church's worship. They are part of the family that is worshipping.

Churches do this differently. Some keep children in the whole service, some have a children's program for part of it, and many offer both. Whatever your church does, a few things help. Sit where your child can see. Let them hold the songbook, stand for the singing and join the amen. On the way there, tell them one thing to listen for, and on the way home ask what they noticed. The catechism tells a child that the church is God's family who follow Jesus together, and a family has room for its noisy members.

open.label: Not a Building
open.why: A family devotion on the church as people who belong to each other, long before it is a building you go to.

also.label: Question 60: Why do we gather with the church?
also.why: The catechism's short answer for a child on why the church meets: God makes us part of his family, the church.

also.label: Why Does the Bible Call the Church a Family?
also.why: For the parent: why Scripture calls the church a household, and what that means for a family that feels out of place on Sunday.

also.label: Finding a Church
also.why: What Scripture says about finding a church, for a family that has drifted away while the children were small.

sessions.question: What would help your child feel that the church is their family too, and not only yours?
sessions.do: Before church this week, tell your child one thing to listen for. Sit where they can see, let them stand and sing, and on the way home ask what they noticed.

verse.text: Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.

group.open: What do you remember about going to church as a child, if you went at all?
discuss: What does Jesus' indignation at his disciples say about how a church should welcome children?
What makes Sunday hardest with small children in your home?
How could the adults in a church help a parent who is managing small children alone?
group.pray: Pray for families who find Sunday hard, for single parents managing alone in a pew, and for churches to make room for children.

sessions.title: Where is God?
teaching: Sooner or later a small child asks where God is. Sometimes it's simple curiosity, sometimes it comes in the dark, and sometimes it comes after a grandparent dies or a pet is buried in the garden. The catechism's answer for a child is honest: we cannot see God, but he has shown us who he is in Jesus. You don't need to explain more than the child is asking. Say that God is everywhere, that nowhere is too far for him, and that he became one of us in Jesus so that we could know what he is like.

The psalmist asked the same question and found it turned the other way round: “Where can I go to escape Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence?” (Psalm 139:7). A small child doesn't need a proof. They need to know that God is near when the light goes out, and that you trust him too. The film this session opens was made for children of seven and up, so watch it first, then tell the youngest its answer in your own words. A child's faith isn't finished at six, and it was never a parent's to finish.

open.label: Why can't I see God?
open.why: A short film in seven pictures on why no one sees God with their eyes, and how he has made himself known, most of all in Jesus.

also.label: Question 67: How do we know God is real if we cannot see him?
also.why: The catechism's answer for a child who wants to see God, with a verse to read together and a short prayer.

also.label: Psalm 139, passage by passage
also.why: The psalm of a God who is everywhere and knows us before we are born, with plain-words notes, to read at bedtime in pieces.

also.label: Faith with children, ages 7 to 11
also.why: The next track on the road, in Faith at Home: Faith with children, ages 7 to 11. Take it up when this one has settled.

sessions.question: When your child asks where God is, what do you most want them to hear in your answer?
sessions.do: When your child next asks where God is, answer in two sentences: God is everywhere, and he showed us what he is like in Jesus. Then read Psalm 139:7-10 together at bedtime.

verse.text: If I rise on the wings of the dawn, if I settle by the farthest sea, even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast.

care: Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Where did you picture God being, when you were very small?
discuss: Why might a small child's question about where God is really be a question about whether they are safe?
How does Jesus change the answer a parent can give to a child who wants to see God?
Looking back over these eight sessions, what has changed in your home, and what will you keep doing?
group.pray: Give thanks for the small children in each home, and pray that they would grow up knowing God is near, through every age still ahead of them.
